issues.issue: "[A]s often as may be deemed expedient" does not say by whom expediency is judged or by what standard. The phrase is vague but it merely preserves rights rather than creating an obligation.

The clause speaks of a breach "by any party" waived "by the other party so empowered to act," although this Guaranty imposes obligations only on the Guarantor and section 4.4 requires waivers to be signed by MTC. The reciprocal phrasing is loose rather than genuinely ambiguous.

The thirty-day fallback cure period in A runs from notice "to Network Operator," while section 2.5 gives Guarantor a cure right measured by the Network Operator Agreement and section 2.6 promises Guarantor contemporaneous notice. Whether Guarantor gets the same thirty days is not stated.

The clause makes the Agreement binding upon and inuring to the benefit of "Network Operator," which is not a signatory to this Guaranty (see the preamble, which names only Guarantor and MTC as parties). Whether Network Operator has rights or duties under the Guaranty is left unclear.
Section 4.6 separately restates severability ("in such cases the principle of Severability shall govern"), duplicating this section. The duplication is redundant rather than contradictory.

Amendments and waivers are effective only if "in writing and signed by MTC," omitting any signature by the Guarantor even for amendments that would enlarge its obligations. Whether a one-signature amendment can bind the Guarantor is a question the wording invites.

Notices must be "sent via overnight courier or personally delivered," an exclusive two-method list that excludes mail, fax and email; whether a notice given another way is ineffective is left to inference. The listing invites an expressio unius argument.

"[E]ffective the business day following the date sent delivered via overnight courier" is garbled — "sent delivered" leaves it unclear whether effectiveness runs from dispatch or from delivery. The one-day rule turns on which event starts it.

The clause refers to the laws of the "State of Massachusetts," which is styled a Commonwealth in the preamble; the slip is immaterial to meaning. "[G]overned by, construed in and enforced in accordance exclusively with" is otherwise a standard, definite choice of law.

Arbitration is conditioned on the parties failing "to resolve any dispute between them through mediation" or being "unable to convene mediation within 60 days of first attempting to do so," yet nothing in this Guaranty provides for mediation, identifies who must initiate it, or defines what counts as "first attempting" it. Whether the condition precedent was satisfied turns wholly on those undefined phrases.

The clause makes arbitration available only "at MTC's sole election" and permits consolidation with the MTC/Network Operator arbitration, which is difficult to reconcile with the next sentence's default that "all disputes shall be resolved by litigation" and with the wholesale incorporation of the Network Operator Agreement's dispute resolution provisions in the last sentence of section 4.6. Which regime governs a given dispute must be construed.

The litigation default is expressly subordinated to MTC's arbitration election in the preceding sentence, but the last sentence of section 4.6 incorporates "all other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration" from the Network Operator Agreement, which may itself mandate arbitration. The two cannot be applied together without deciding which controls.

"Except to the extent MTC elects arbitration ... for a given dispute" gives no timing or manner for the election, so the forum for any dispute remains indeterminate until MTC acts. The phrase "a given dispute" also leaves open whether a single controversy can be split between forums.

"All other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration" in a separate agreement are incorporated without identifying them, so the reach of "relating to" and the meaning of "other" (other than what?) are open. A court must decide which terms of the Network Operator Agreement came across.

The incorporated provisions may conflict with the express terms of section 4.6 itself — MTC's sole election to arbitrate, the Boston AAA venue, the expedited Commercial Rules, and the Middlesex County litigation default — and the clause gives no order of precedence. That is a direct conflict within the same section.
